AI can already cut, caption and format a clip for you. Free GitHub skills teach Claude the editing part in minutes. So why isn't everyone going viral off podcast clips? Because editing was never the hard part. Choosing the moment is. AI does not know which 47 seconds out of a two hour conversation deserve to become the clip. No context. No content intelligence. Here is how you build that layer. Scrape the latest 100 clips from the biggest podcast short form accounts. Steven Bartlett, Chris Williamson, Alex Hormozi, anyone running serious long form volume. Capture views, post date, duration, transcript, text overlay and format. Then scrape their original long form episodes and pull the complete transcripts with timestamps. The timestamps are non negotiable. They are what lets Claude match every clip back to the exact episode and the exact moment it came from. Now you reverse engineer the decision. Why those 47 seconds. Where the clip starts. What context got removed. Whether the payoff moved forward. What spoken hook, text overlay and format they used. And how it performed against that account's normal clips. Run enough of these and the patterns surface. Turn the patterns into a Claude skill that understands how the best podcast teams select and package their clips. Then hand it any new timestamped transcript. It returns the strongest moments, exact timestamps, hook options, text overlays, formats and editing instructions. The editing skill does the easy part. None of this needs new software. The tools exist. The clipping skills exist. The data is public. Nobody is assembling it into an intelligence layer. Impossible to fail does not mean every clip goes viral. It means every clip starts with real evidence, and every result makes the next selection smarter. Build the selection layer first. The edit is the easy bit.

The 8 steps from chatting with AI to building AI systems How to learn AI automation step by step, from using ChatGPT or Claude every day to building AI systems for a real business. Building means AI is connected to the tools a business runs on and does a real job inside a workflow. Use AI every day and learn where it's wrong. It's great at drafting and sorting. It slips on exact numbers, dates, and facts you never gave it. Structured output (JSON). Ask for the answer in fixed boxes: name, company, invoice number, amount, deadline, priority. Leave a box empty if the info isn't there. A spreadsheet or CRM can use boxes. It can't use a paragraph. Automation. A tool like n8n or Zapier moves those boxes into your tools: the billing sheet, the help desk ticket, the customer reply. Human in the loop. Refunds, anything with money, customers, or that you can't undo, waits for your approval. Document and image reading (OCR). AI reads receipts, invoices, delivery slips and forms and fills the same boxes. A total that doesn't add up goes to a person. AI agents. Give it a goal. It works in a loop, takes a step, checks the result, picks the next step. Use agents where the steps change every time. Multiple AIs with checkers. One AI does the work, a second checks it against your rules (is the refund under your limit, does the reply sound like you). If a check fails, the work goes back or comes to you. Plain formulas handle the math. See the whole system. Look at a business's CRM, shared drive, inbox and online store, and know where AI fits, where it doesn't, and which kind of model each job needs: small and fast for sorting, bigger for contracts, image-capable for receipts. Works for small businesses, agencies, online stores, clinics, contractors, bookkeepers and office teams. If you don't know where you are on this ladder and want to learn all of it, I have step-by-step video courses inside my community that take you from complete beginner to building AI systems.
